newsitem.title: UK: Mitchell says will remain N.Irish peace talks head.
newsitem.headline: Mitchell says will remain N.Irish peace talks head.

text.p: Former U.S. senator George Mitchell on Monday dismissed reports that he was considering resigning as chairman of current Northern Ireland peace talks, the biggest effort in decades to end sectarian conflict.

"No, that is completely untrue," Mitchell told reporters when asked about reports that he would pull out of the talks unless progress is made on how to disarm Irish Catholic and pro-British Protestant guerrilla groups.

The talks, which resumed on Monday after a summer break, have failed to tackle a single substantive issue since they began in June and have turned into a replay of the Protestant-Catholic rivalry at the root of the conflict.
Mitchell said he was happy to be back and stressed his commitment to the talks, aimed at ending communal distrust after a 25-year guerrilla war.

"When I accepted the invitation of the (British and Irish) to participate in these talks, I accepted enthusiastically because I believed the talks represent an historic opportunity for the people of Northen Ireland. That is still my view," Mitchell said in a statement.

The opening day of the talks were dominated by squabbling over an attempt by hardline pro-British leader Ian Paisley to have two smaller Protestant parties linked to guerrilla groups expelled from the talks.

Paisley, leader of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), was angry beause the parties have failed to condemn a threat by pro-British guerrillas to kill convicted Protestant activist Billy Wright, who opposes their participation in the talks.
Wright says the talks could lead to an all-Ireland state against the wishes of the British region's Protestant majority.
"We as a party are not prepared to continued at the table until this matter is resolved," Paisley told reporters.
The Progressive Unionist Party and Ulster Democratic Party say they have no control over the activities of Protestant guerrillas who have maintained a shaky ceasefire since October 1994.
PUP spokesman David Ervine said:" We have commitment to the talks...and to peace in our society...I am fairly confident of the strength of our defence."
The British and Irish governments regard the presence of the two Loyalist parties as crucial in securing new political agreement.

Sinn Fein, which won a 15.5 percent voting share at a pre-talks election, is barred from participation because its IRA guerilla wing, which is fighting British rule, refuses to renew a truce that collapsed in February.
